entries.clue: Arranged numbers in very quick time to visit house in South of France (8)

indicatorNotes.to visit: To visit a house is to go inside it, so the letters that call round end up within the house's name rather than beside it.

blocks.note: a mas is a Provençal farmhouse, the ordinary word for a country house in the south of France
something done in very quick time is done in a trice

annotation.surface: Sums worked at speed while calling on a farmhouse in Provence.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition wants numbers set out in rows and columns, the way a mathematician arranges them. 'Mas' is the Provençal farmhouse and turns up whenever a clue mentions the south of France.
annotation.definitionFit: These are rectangular arrays of numbers written out in rows and columns, which is precisely numbers arranged.

entries.clue: Dread anonymous compilers (3)

blocks.note: a = anonymous, the abbreviation printed where an author's name would go
people who compile crosswords refer to themselves in their own clues as 'we'

annotation.surface: Nameless crossword setters and the fear they inspire.
annotation.walkthrough: Setters speaking of themselves as 'we' is the convention doing the work, and it is worth owning: 'compiler', 'setter' and 'this writer' all point at the same two letters. An unsigned piece is 'anon', shortened once more to its initial.
annotation.definitionFit: Dread is the older sense of the word, the shrinking fear before something overwhelming that survives in 'awestruck' and 'God-fearing'.

entries.clue: The Indian side inform on Australian touring India (5)

indicatorNotes.touring: A tour goes round the country it visits, so the letters doing the touring close around the one named.

blocks.note: to rat on somebody is to inform on them
a = Australian, the usual abbreviation
India is I in the radio alphabet

annotation.surface: A cricket team telling tales about an Australian player during a tour of India.
annotation.walkthrough: Every cricketing word is doing a different job underneath: the side is a dish, the tour is an instruction. India as I comes from the radio alphabet, which setters raid for single letters from Alpha to Zulu.
annotation.definitionFit: Raita is the cool yoghurt-and-cucumber dish served alongside a curry, so it is the side that comes with an Indian meal rather than a team.

entries.clue: Their chosen meal flies (10)

indicatorNotes.flies: What flies is up in the air and out of any fixed order, so the letters it acts on come down arranged differently.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: Some creature's preferred dinner taking to the air.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words describe the creatures and hand over their letters at the same time, which is what makes the clue work twice. Their dinner is taken out of the air with a tongue longer than the body it shoots from.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: these colour-changing lizards live on insects caught on the wing, so their chosen meal really does fly.

entries.clue: Temper shown by son many times (6)

blocks.note: s = son, the abbreviation on a family tree
doing something many times is doing it often

annotation.surface: A boy's repeated displays of bad temper.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Temper' is the verb here, not the noun the surface offers: to temper a remark is to take the edge off it. Steel is tempered the same way, heated and cooled until it stops being brittle.
annotation.definitionFit: To temper something is to moderate it — to take the harshness out of a demand or a judgement — which is what softening it does.

entries.clue: Lugubrious brother invites a few round (6)

indicatorNotes.round: Asking people round means they come and gather about you, so the guests' letters close around the host's.

blocks.note: a few of something is some of it
br = brother, the title written in front of a monk's name

annotation.surface: A gloomy man having a handful of friends over.
annotation.walkthrough: The invitation is the instruction: guests who come round arrive about their host, not after him. 'Brother' shortens to the two letters of the religious title.
annotation.definitionFit: Lugubrious and sombre both name a settled, funereal gloom rather than a passing bad mood.

entries.clue: Louis XIV briefly ruined? (4)

indicatorNotes.briefly: Given briefly, a two-word title is cut short, and here the second word shrinks to the letter it starts with.

blocks.note: Louis XIV of France took the sun as his emblem, which is where his English nickname comes from, and this is its first word
the KING of the same nickname, docked by 'briefly' to its initial

annotation.surface: A long reign told in short, and a king who came to a bad end.
annotation.walkthrough: The nickname belongs to the French king who styled himself le Roi Soleil and sat on the throne for seventy-two years. The question mark admits the definition is figurative: nothing has gone under the water.
annotation.definitionFit: A scheme that is sunk has gone down and cannot be raised again, the same finality as calling it ruined.

entries.clue: Bumped into Rat in London suburbs (9)

annotation.definitionNote: The answer is a single name for a whole stretch of suburbs, so the plural definition covers what one singular word holds.

blocks.note: to bump into somebody is to meet them by chance
Roland Rat was the glove-puppet rodent who became a star of British breakfast television in 1983

annotation.surface: A chance encounter with a rodent out in the further reaches of London.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital R is the only warning that the rat has a first name. The Metropolitan Railway coined the word for the countryside it ran trains through and then sold houses in, from Wembley out to Amersham.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the name for the north-west London suburbs that grew up along the Metropolitan line, sold to commuters as half country, half town.

entries.clue: Frenchman persuaded one brewing tea to come back to the table (11)

indicatorNotes.brewing: Tea brewing is stirred and steeped until it is nothing like what went in, and letters given that treatment come out in another order.

blocks.note: René is the crossword's stock French first name
to get somebody to do something is to persuade them into it
i = one, the Roman numeral
the three letters of TEA in a new order

annotation.surface: A Frenchman talking someone into making a fresh pot before talks resume.
annotation.walkthrough: Coming back to the table is diplomatic idiom, not furniture: it is what two sides do when a deal has fallen apart. Four separate pieces in a row make this one of the puzzle's longest assemblies.
annotation.definitionFit: Parties who come back to the table are reopening terms they had already settled, which is exactly what the answer means.

entries.clue: Keep adjusting a focusing device (6)

indicatorNotes.adjusting: Adjusting something shifts its parts about, and the parts being shifted here are the six letters given.

blocks.note: to keep something is to retain it

annotation.surface: Fiddling with the focus on a camera.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Keep' reads first as the tower of a castle and second as the verb the clue needs. The image arrives here upside down and the brain turns it back the right way up.
annotation.definitionFit: The retina is the light-sensitive screen at the back of the eye, the surface onto which the lens brings the picture into focus.

entries.clue: Make small improvement to well-crafted melody (4-4)

blocks.note: fine work is well-crafted work
a melody is a tune

annotation.surface: Touching up a nicely written song.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves are plain synonyms and the enumeration's hyphen shows exactly where they join. The expression comes from radio sets, where a separate knob nudged the dial a fraction at a time.
annotation.definitionFit: To fine-tune something is to make the last small adjustments that improve it, rather than to overhaul it.

entries.clue: On board, one depressed to flee island … (6,3)

blocks.note: to flee is to escape
a key is a low island, as in the Florida Keys

annotation.surface: A passenger low in spirits aboard a boat, longing to get off an island.
annotation.walkthrough: The board is a keyboard and 'depressed' is a finger pushing down, not a mood. The definition then runs straight on into the wordplay, so the words that give the letters also finish the description.
annotation.definitionFit: A keyboard is a board of keys, pressing one is depressing it, and this is the key at the top left that gets you out of things.

entries.clue: Saint revealing a freshly-composed prayer (5,6)

indicatorNotes.freshly-composed: Something composed afresh is put together again out of the same parts in a new arrangement.

blocks.note: s = saint, the abbreviation in front of a church's name
anagram fodder, ten letters, with the saint's S joined on

annotation.surface: A saint letting slip a brand new prayer.
annotation.walkthrough: The prayer is the Latin antiphon beginning 'Hail, holy Queen', sung to Mary at the close of the day and at Catholic funerals. Latin titles like this are fair fodder in a British daily, which assumes the church calendar as general knowledge.
annotation.definitionFit: It is the Marian antiphon said at the end of the rosary and sung over the coffin at a requiem — a prayer in the plainest sense.

entries.clue: … hard to get right out of depression (5)

indicatorNotes.out of: Taking one thing out of another leaves the second short of it, so the letter named is dropped from the word that follows.

blocks.note: a trough is a depression, the dip between two ridges
r = right, the abbreviation on a map or a stage direction

annotation.surface: Hauling yourself up out of low spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: The dots carry the surface over from the clue before, where somebody was depressed; here depression is a dip in the ground or a weather chart. The definition sits alone at the front, where the run-on sentence hides it.
annotation.definitionFit: A tough job and a hard job are the same thing: work that takes real effort to get through.

entries.clue: Ordinary visitor comes in to criticise part of Evil Empire (5,5)

indicatorNotes.comes in to: Somebody who comes in to a room is inside it once they arrive, so the letters named sit within the word that follows.

blocks.note: to rate somebody is to scold them, the old sense behind 'berate'
o = ordinary, as in the old O-level
a visitor you put up is a guest

annotation.surface: An unremarkable visitor dropping in to find fault.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Criticise' wants the old sense of rate — to tear a strip off somebody — not to score out of ten. Reagan called the Soviet Union the evil empire in 1983, and the rhetoric has been recycled for outlaw countries ever since.
annotation.definitionFit: A rogue state is a country the West treats as an outlaw, the kind of member an 'evil empire' would be assembled from.

entries.clue: Hang around Ohio, opening an American volume (6)

indicatorNotes.opening: Opening something makes a gap in it, and the letter named drops straight into the gap.

blocks.note: liter is the American spelling of the metric measure of volume
o = Ohio, the state's single-letter abbreviation

annotation.surface: Idling in Ohio over the first pages of an American book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Volume' is the measure rather than the book the surface offers, and the American spelling drops the final e onto the r. Ohio's single letter predates the postal code that made it OH.
annotation.definitionFit: To loiter is to hang around a place with no business being there, the word on every 'no loitering' sign.

entries.clue: Breaking up during April I find exhilarating (9)

indicatorNotes.Breaking up: Breaking something up splits it open, and the letter named wedges itself into the split.

blocks.note: April falls in spring, so anything happening during it happens in spring
the pronoun itself, one letter long

annotation.surface: Somebody cheerfully announcing that April is the month to end a relationship.
annotation.walkthrough: Breaking up is a couple splitting on the surface and an instruction underneath. Schools break up too, which is the reading the month quietly supports.
annotation.definitionFit: Something inspiring lifts you and makes you want to act, the same buoyant effect as calling it exhilarating.

entries.clue: For Lithuanian, Latvian is sort of blue (6)

blocks.note: co- is the prefix for a fellow anything, and from a Lithuanian's point of view the man next door is a fellow one
a Balt is a native of Latvia, Lithuania or Estonia, the three Baltic states

annotation.surface: One Baltic nationality described from a neighbour's point of view.
annotation.walkthrough: The joke is a hyphenated word hiding in the first three: seen from Vilnius, the man from Riga is a fellow Balt. The blue is the pigment ground from the metal, deep and faintly violet.
annotation.definitionFit: Cobalt names a particular shade of blue, the strong slightly purple colour of the pigment made from the metal of the same name.

entries.clue: Stopping heading off and tailing off (6)

indicatorNotes.heading off: A word heading off loses its head, and a word's head is the letter it begins with.

blocks.note: stopping something is ceasing it, and the C at the front is what heads off

annotation.surface: Blocking someone's departure while their resolve fades.
annotation.walkthrough: Two 'off's doing two different jobs is the whole disguise: the first lops a letter, the second belongs to the definition. Both halves of the clue are present participles, so neither looks more like a definition than the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Rain or noise tailing off is lessening bit by bit, which is what easing describes.

entries.clue: Cold plain fish medic tucks into (6)

indicatorNotes.tucks into: Tucking into a meal is getting right inside it, so the letters that tuck in sit within the food's name.

blocks.note: the tinned fish, crosswordland's standard four-letter one
dr = doctor

annotation.surface: A doctor making a hearty start on a plate of fish.
annotation.walkthrough: Tucking in is the diner's phrase and the container instruction in one. The cold plain is the treeless Arctic ground whose subsoil never thaws.
annotation.definitionFit: Tundra is the flat treeless land of the far north, frozen hard below the surface all year — a cold plain in the plainest sense.

entries.clue: University gown brought round, one’s forced under it (6)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition describes the answer instead of naming a synonym: 'it' stands for the entry, and what a person is forced to act under is this.

indicatorNotes.brought round: Something brought round is fetched about the thing in the middle, so its letters close around the letter named.

blocks.note: a gown is a dress
u = university, as written in Oxford U

annotation.surface: An academic gown fetched over for somebody who is being made to wear it.
annotation.walkthrough: A comma is all that divides the wordplay from a definition that offers no synonym at all, only a sentence the answer completes. Acting under duress is the legal plea of having had no real choice.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody who signs under duress has been forced into it by threats, and that pressure is what the clue's 'it' points at.

entries.clue: Vlad rejecting Indian meal? What are the odds then? (5)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a pet form of the man's first name, Vladimir, standing in for the surname the grid wants.

indicatorNotes.rejecting: To reject something is to throw it back, and letters thrown back come out in the opposite order.
indicatorNotes.What are the odds then?: The odds are the odd-numbered positions — first, third, fifth and so on — so only the letters standing in those places are kept.

blocks.note: the two words written backwards run LAEMNAIDNI, whose first, third, fifth, seventh and ninth letters spell the entry

annotation.surface: A man turning down a curry and asking what the chances are.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Indian meal' is the raw material itself, letters and all, not a cue to name a dish. 'Vlad' is the everyday shortening of Vladimir, the first name that goes with the surname wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: The Bolshevik leader was Vladimir Ilyich, so the chummy short form of that first name points at the surname he is known by.

entries.clue: Be frightened, knight: crusader’s rampaging about (3,6)

indicatorNotes.rampaging about: Something rampaging about charges off in every direction, and letters doing that finish in a different order.

blocks.note: n = knight, the piece's symbol on a chess scoresheet
anagram fodder, eight letters, with the knight's N joined on

annotation.surface: A warning shouted to a knight as a crusader charges about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Knight' looks like more of the crusading scenery and is really the chessboard's N. The apostrophe-s is just 'is', holding the sentence together.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody running scared is acting out of fear of what is coming, which is being frightened rather than literally running anywhere.

entries.clue: Neighbour with empty stomach is close (5)

indicatorNotes.stomach: A stomach sits in the middle of the body, so whatever goes there goes into the middle of the word rather than either end.

blocks.note: to abut something is to neighbour it, to share a boundary with it
empty means nothing, and nothing is written as the round letter

annotation.surface: A hungry neighbour standing nearby.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Empty' as the hollow letter is a convention worth owning, and it turns up as 'nothing', 'love' and 'duck' too. 'Close' is the adverb of approximation — close to nine, about nine — not the verb or the airless room.
annotation.definitionFit: 'About twenty' and 'close to twenty' say the same thing: both put you near the figure without landing on it.

entries.clue: Worry, losing the last bit of spare time (4)

indicatorNotes.losing the last bit of: Losing its last bit docks a word of its final letter and leaves everything in front of it.

blocks.note: spare time is free time, and FREE gives up its final letter
t = time, the symbol in any physics equation

annotation.surface: Worrying as the last of your free time disappears.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spare time' reads as one phrase and then splits, the adjective and the noun going to different jobs. To fret is to keep gnawing at a worry rather than to panic once.
annotation.definitionFit: Worry is the verb sense: to fret is to keep turning something over anxiously, the small continuous kind of alarm.

entries.clue: Lie prostrated with grief: this is so delicate (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The entry is a noun and the definition an adjective phrase; the word is used attributively of anything as fine as the metalwork it names.

indicatorNotes.prostrated: Somebody prostrated is thrown flat and laid out anyhow, and letters treated that way come up in a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, three letters
anagram fodder, five more letters

annotation.surface: A mourner lying face down, undone by sorrow.
annotation.walkthrough: Grief prostrates the mourner on the surface and rearranges the letters underneath. The craft meant is gold or silver wire twisted and soldered into tracery as fine as lace.
annotation.definitionFit: The word names jeweller's work in wire so fine it looks like lace, and it is applied to anything else of that delicacy.

entries.clue: Animal in a painful condition essentially fit (6)

indicatorNotes.essentially: The essence of a word is its very centre, so only the letter standing in the middle is taken.

blocks.note: the article itself, taken as read
gout is the painful swelling of the joints, proverbially of the big toe
the middle letter of FIT

annotation.surface: A creature in poor health that is nonetheless basically well.
annotation.walkthrough: The contradiction is the disguise: ailing but essentially fit sounds like a vet's report and is two separate instructions. The creature is a long-legged rodent of Central and South America, a cousin of the guinea pig.
annotation.definitionFit: The agouti is a rabbit-sized rodent of the New World tropics, so the category word is the plainest possible definition.

entries.clue: Pitch that a rainstorm covers (3)

indicatorNotes.covers: What covers something lies over it and hides it, so the letters wanted are buried under the words themselves.

blocks.note: the last letter of the first word, all of the second and the opening of the third, read straight on

annotation.surface: A road surface out in the rain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' is the black stuff here, not the sports field or the throw or the note. Three-letter hidden answers can sit across two word-joins like this and still be almost invisible.
annotation.definitionFit: Pitch and tar are both the sticky black residue boiled out of wood or coal and used to seal roads, roofs and ships' timbers.

entries.clue: Pet suppressing cry of disgust when grabbed (6)

indicatorNotes.suppressing: To suppress a noise is to keep it down inside you, so the cry named is held within the other word.

blocks.note: the commonest household pet
ugh is the noise made at something revolting

annotation.surface: An animal swallowing its objection at being picked up.
annotation.walkthrough: Pets do get grabbed, so the definition hides inside a scene it belongs to. The cry is one of those spellings that exist only in comic strips and crosswords.
annotation.definitionFit: To be caught is to be seized and held, by a hand round the middle or by the police.

entries.clue: Be dazed by what you may do on a clear night out (3,5)

annotation.definition2: what you may do on a clear night out

blocks.note: the state after a blow to the head, with points of light swimming in front of the eyes

blocks.clueFragment: what you may do on a clear night out
blocks.note: standing outdoors under a cloudless sky with your head tipped back

annotation.surface: Being knocked silly by an evening of stargazing.
annotation.walkthrough: One word of joinery welds the two definitions into a single sentence, which is what hides the seam. The dazed sense is boxing's, for the flashes that follow a punch.
annotation.definitionFit: A blow to the head is said to make you see stars, and on a cloudless night outdoors you do the same thing literally.
